headline: Southwest Ledge Cold and Green — Fluke Still Biting, Albies Running Wild on the Harvest Moon
subhead: Bigger tides around the rips are stacking bait and stirring up one of the best late-September stretches Block Island has seen in years.
body_markdown:
There's a smell to the air out here this week that tells you more than any forecast — that first cut of cold on the northwest wind mixing with the warm push still coming off the Gulf Stream edge. You feel it standing on the Old Harbor breakwater before you see it: the water's still holding summer color and warmth, but the wind has that fall bite. That collision is exactly what's been driving this bite, and it's why the last several days around the island have been some of the best fishing of the whole season, not the worst, even as we tip into the back half of September.

The Harvest Moon tides have kicked the current up around Southwest Ledge and the North Rip, and that extra push has done what it always does out here — it's concentrated bait against structure and turned rips that were lazy in August into legitimate feeding lanes again. Bunker schools, some of them adult-sized, have been working through the rips on the last of the ebb and first of the flood, and every predator in the neighborhood has taken notice. Stripers are stacking under and around those schools, bluefish are slashing through the edges, and the false albacore and bonito — which showed up strong last week — haven't slowed down one bit. We flagged that pattern last week, said the albie and bonito push would hold with the tide and moon lining up, and that's exactly what's happened. If anything it's built.

Fluke are the story nobody expected to still be talking about this late in September. Warmer-than-normal water sitting over the sand and gravel humps off the west side and around the Great Salt Pond entrance has kept fluke shallower and more active than they have any business being this time of year. Charter boats working 30 to 50 feet off the west side are still putting keepers in the box on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails drifted slow with the tide. The better fish have been coming on the last two hours of the incoming, when the current softens just enough to keep bait near bottom without dragging the boat off the structure too fast.

Striped bass fishing has been building steadily rather than exploding, which is honestly the more sustainable pattern this time of year. The Southwest Ledge continues to hold fish, particularly on the down-tide side where the current breaks over the rock pile in 20 to 35 feet. Live eels fished on a simple three-way rig, or bucktails bounced along bottom on the drift, have been the most consistent producers. The North Rip has been more of a dawn-and-dusk program — the bigger fish are using low light to move up onto the shallower structure and ambush bunker pods getting pushed around by current. A handful of fish in the 30-to-40-pound class have come off the Rip on bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the last hour of daylight, though the bite has been more about quality than volume. Anyone expecting a wide-open blitz every trip is going to be disappointed; this has been a pick-your-window fishery, and the window has mostly been tide-change to tide-change, not all-day.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun on the bunker the way they always do this time of year, and the size has ticked up noticeably from what we were seeing in August. Casting poppers and metal — Hopkins or Kastmasters in the 2-to-3-ounce range — into surface blitzes around the rips has been producing quick, violent action when the schools show. That intensifying pattern is exactly what we expected as more bait gets pushed south and east on these bigger tides, and it's held true through the week.

The albie and bonito bite deserves its own mention because it's genuinely been the highlight for a lot of boats. Both species have been working bait pods tight against current lines off the Ledge and around the east side of the island, and small profile epoxy jigs — half-ounce to one-ounce — worked with a fast, erratic retrieve have been the go-to. Bonito especially have wanted a smaller offering than most anglers start with; downsizing from a typical albie jig has made a real difference on the tougher afternoons when the fish get finicky.

Porgies remain a dependable, if unglamorous, option for anyone wanting fresh fillets without chasing structure-specific bass or fickle albies. Sea worms and clam on standard porgy rigs around the rock piles off Southwest Point have kept producing steady numbers in 15 to 25 feet.

Looking ahead, the next several days should keep this pattern intact. The Harvest Moon's tidal push isn't fading yet, and as long as the wind stays manageable out of the northwest rather than swinging hard onshore, expect the fluke, albie, and bass bite to hold together. If there's a shift coming, it'll arrive with the first real cold front of the fall — that's the thing to watch. Until then, fish the tide changes hard around the Ledge and the Rip, keep bait sizes on the smaller side for the albies, and don't be surprised if the biggest bass of the week come after dark on bunker chunks fished patiently on the bottom.
